meta.title: Who really said "If we don't end war, war will end us"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, H. G. Wells wrote it — as John Cabal's line in his 1936 film Things to Come, not in The War of the Worlds or The New World Order as often claimed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If we don't end war, war will end us'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely H. G. Wells — from his screenplay for the 1936 film Things to Come, spoken by John Cabal. It is not from his novels, despite the covers.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1866–1946 · English novelist & screenwriter of “Things to Come”
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Wells: he wrote the line for his screenplay of the 1936 film Things to Come ↗, where the protagonist John Cabal (Raymond Massey) speaks it in a Christmas-1940 scene on the eve of war. Wells had already adapted the screenplay into a book in 1935. The wording circulating online matches the film exactly — only the source usually cited (his novels, or The New World Order) is wrong.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Feature film; screenplay by H. G. Wells (released 20 February 1936). Wells adapted it into a book in 1935.
John Cabal (played by Raymond Massey), in the Christmas-1940 opening scene
Wells’s 1933 novel The Shape of Things to Come

source.excerpt:
— War doesn’t stop progress. It stimulates progress.
— But you can overdo a stimulant… If we don’t end war, war will end us.
— Peace on earth, goodwill towards men. Real old-fashioned Christmas this year.
trail: The exact sentence appears in the Things to Come (1936) script ↗, spoken during the opening Christmas scene.
H. G. Wells wrote the screenplay himself, adapting his 1933 novel; the film was released 20 February 1936 and he turned the script into a book in 1935 — per Wikipedia ↗.
It is not in The New World Order (1940), where quote sites often place it: the full text ↗ contains no such sentence.
Publishers have printed the line on covers of The War of the Worlds and War and the Future, though it appears in neither book.
source.excerptNote: From the Christmas-Day exchange that opens the film, as Everytown argues over whether another war is coming. Cabal, Wells’s mouthpiece, cuts through the optimism with the warning.

source.rightsNote: The line comes from Wells’s screenplay for Things to Come, released as a film in 1936 and published by Wells as a book in 1935 — both well after 1931, so under US copyright. Wells died in 1946; literary rights rest with his estate, and the film with London Film Productions (Alexander Korda).

author.heading: About H. G. Wells
author.metaLine: 1866–1946 · English novelist, historian & prophet of science fiction
author.bio: Herbert George Wells (1866–1946) was an English writer often called a father of science fiction, author of The War of the Worlds, The Time Machine and The Outline of History. A lifelong campaigner for world government, he wrote the screenplay for the 1936 film Things to Come, adapting his own 1933 novel The Shape of Things to Come — the source of this line.

misattribution.heading: The mix-up
misattribution.intro: The words are really Wells’s — but almost every citation points at the wrong book, and the line is usually stripped of the film scene that gave it meaning.

items.who: The War of the Worlds / War and the Future
items.why: Reprint publishers have splashed the line across covers of these titles (e.g. a paperback sold as “The War of the Worlds: If we don’t end war, war will end us”), implying it comes from the novel. It does not appear in either work.
Quote databases sometimes cite “The New World Order, p. 114.” The complete 1940 text ↗ contains no sentence of the kind.
It travels as a bare maxim on quote sites, detached from its origin as dialogue in a science-fiction film about the coming world war.

misattribution.truthLine: The real home of the line is John Cabal’s warning in Wells’s Things to Come (1936) ↗ — genuine Wells, wrong source almost everywhere else.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Wells wrote Things to Come as a warning dressed as prophecy. Its opening act imagines “Everytown” sliding into a devastating world war beginning at Christmas 1940 — a year before the real war would engulf Britain. Cabal’s line lands in that scene as the sober counter to neighbours insisting another war could never come, or could only spur progress.

The film’s whole argument — that unchecked war would wreck civilisation and that only a rational world order could save it — grew out of Wells’s long campaign for world government, the same conviction behind his 1940 Declaration of the Rights of Man. The one-liner survives; the film that framed it is largely forgotten.
